evidence: Findings from cited literature on human parent-infant interaction

claim: When infants receive contingent adult feedback for their speech-like utterances, they tend to produce more speech-like vocalizations.
source: This can initiate a positive feedback loop: when infants receive contingent adult feedback for their speech-like utterances, they tend to produce more speech-like vocalizations (Goldstein and Schwade, 2008; Warlaumont et al., 2014).

claim: Babbling in humans is hypothesized to serve as a vocal fitness signal, potentially evolved to elicit more parental care.
source: Babbling in humans is also hypothesized to serve as a vocal fitness signal, potentially evolved to elicit more parental care thus, gaining importance throughout human evolution (Oller et al., 2016).

claim: Maternal social feedback shapes different aspects of the vocal practice and learning of pups.
source: In conclusion, our study shows that maternal social feedback shapes different aspects of the vocal practice and learning of pups.

claim: Bats share key aspects of human brain architecture and vocal development.
source: As bats are highly social mammals that share key aspects of human brain architecture and vocal development, our findings will substantially advance our knowledge about how social interactions shape vocal learning.

claim: Saccopteryx bilineata roosts in perennial stable groups, that is colonies.
source: Saccopteryx bilineata roosts in perennial stable groups, that is colonies (Tannenbaum, 1975).
evidence: Description of social structure with citation

claim: Females synchronize the birth of a single pup around the beginning of the rainy season.
source: Females synchronize the birth of a single pup around the beginning of the rainy season (i.e. May).

claim: Pups are weaned at 10–12 weeks of age.
source: Pups are weaned at 10–12 weeks of age (Tannenbaum, 1975).
evidence: Description of developmental timeline with citation

claim: Day-roosts of Saccopteryx bilineata are located in tree cavities or outer walls of man-made structures.
source: Day-roosts of S. bilineata are located in tree cavities or outer walls of man-made structures (Yancey et al., 1998).
evidence: Description of roosting habitat with citation

claim: Saccopteryx bilineata is very light-tolerant.
source: Saccopteryx bilineata is very light-tolerant and most social interactions (e.g. courtship, territorial defense, babbling behavior) occur during the day within the roost (Behr and von Helversen, 2004; Fernandez et al., 2021; Knörnschild et al., 2006).
evidence: Description of species characteristic with citations

claim: Most social interactions in Saccopteryx bilineata occur during the day within the roost.
source: Saccopteryx bilineata is very light-tolerant and most social interactions (e.g. courtship, territorial defense, babbling behavior) occur during the day within the roost (Behr and von Helversen, 2004; Fernandez et al., 2021; Knörnschild et al., 2006).
evidence: Description of behavioral ecology with citations

claim: Individuals in the day-roost maintain an inter-individual distance of 5–8 cm.
source: Individuals in the day-roost maintain an inter-individual distance of 5–8 cm (Voigt et al., 2008).

claim: Only pups are allowed to ignore the inter-individual distance without eliciting aggression.
source: Only pups are allowed to ignore this inter-individual distance without eliciting aggression.

claim: Saccopteryx bilineata possesses a large vocal repertoire (i.e. 25 distinct syllable types) which is fully delineated.
source: This species possesses a large vocal repertoire (i.e. 25 distinct syllable types) which is fully delineated (Behr and von Helversen, 2004; Fernandez et al., 2021; Knörnschild and von Helversen, 2008).
evidence: Description of vocal repertoire with citations

claim: Syllable types in Saccopteryx bilineata are composed into mono- or multisyllabic vocalizations.
source: These syllable types are composed into mono- or multisyllabic vocalizations.

claim: For most vocalizations in Saccopteryx bilineata, the behavioral context and function is known.
source: For most vocalizations, the behavioral context and function is known as well (e.g. the territorial song is an aggressive signal used during territorial defense).

claim: The territorial song is an aggressive signal used during territorial defense.
source: For most vocalizations, the behavioral context and function is known as well (e.g. the territorial song is an aggressive signal used during territorial defense).

claim: Acoustic recordings and observations were recorded ad libitum throughout the pups' ontogeny in their day-roost.
source: Acoustic recordings and observations of social behaviors were recorded ad libitum sensu (Altmann, 1974) throughout the pups' ontogeny (i.e. from birth until weaning) in their day-roost.

claim: In 2016, acoustic recordings and behavioral monitoring were conducted from ten mother-pup dyads belonging to three colonies in the natural reserve Curú in Costa Rica.
source: In 2016, we conducted acoustic recordings and additionally monitored the accompanying behaviors from ten mother-pup dyads belonging to three colonies in the natural reserve Curú in Costa Rica.
evidence: Description of study sample and location

claim: In 2017, acoustic recordings and behavioral observations were conducted from nine mother-pup dyads belonging to three colonies in Gamboa, Panama.
source: In 2017, we likewise conducted acoustic recordings and simultaneous behavioral observations from nine mother-pup dyads belonging to three colonies in Gamboa, a field station of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama.
evidence: Description of study sample and location

claim: Territorial song is produced by adult territorial males daily at dusk and dawn for acoustic territorial defence.
source: Territorial song is produced by adult territorial males daily at dusk and dawn for acoustic territorial defence (Behr and von Helversen, 2004).
evidence: Description of singing behavior with citation

claim: The number of singing males present in a colony was used as a proxy for the amount of social acoustic input a given pup received during its ontogeny.
source: Thus, the number of singing males (i.e. tutors) present in a colony was used as a proxy for the amount of social acoustic input a given pup received during its ontogeny.
